utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Shall we bring in the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Maletic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Maletic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yesterday we left off with some photographs and we're going to continue briefly with three more on the same subject. I'd like us to have a look, please, at 65 ter number 24121.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I should note while we're waiting to see that photograph, Your Honours, I've been in contact with the investigator for the OTP who's responsible for matters dealing with Sarajevo and I'll be able to advise the Court on the provenance of these photographs based on the information I've received from him.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Maletic, this is a view from the roof of Lenjinova 6A which was taken in August 1996. Does this show an area behind the enemy's front line?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be asked whether this is a photograph taken from Lenjinova and from what side of the river it was taken?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably it's the subject you can take up in your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, and I'd like to tender this photograph, please, Your Honours. And with respect to this photograph, the investigator did confirm that this was taken from Lenjinova 6A in August 1996 by an employee of the Office of the Prosecutor at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, can you assist us with a small matter. Now, you described the photograph. You said this is a view from the roof of Lenjinova 6A taken in August, but isn't that evidence you're giving?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What I was doing, Your Honour, in light of Mr. Robinson's concern regarding the provenance of the photograph is I was informing everyone of the provenance of the photograph based on the information I'd received overnight from the Sarajevo investigator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, I should like very much to hear you on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and Judge Baird. Well, you know, we don't dispute when the Prosecution makes a representation. Obviously we know that their representations are always made in good faith and based on facts, but we're not also ready to stipulate to any facts as has been our position from the very beginning of the case. And it's our position that this evidence as to where these photos were taken, number one, should have been brought in the Prosecution's case if they thought it was important and/or can be brought in rebuttal if they're able to convince the Chamber that it meets the standard. But based on the testimony of this witness, we don't see any foundation for admitting the photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed. A rejoinder, Ms. Edgerton, at all?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I just have your indulgence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- I might just want to speak to Mr. Tieger about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Indeed, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I can speak to this, just -- sorry, I can't see Judge Baird.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll move over here, Judge Baird.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Judge Baird, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I principally wanted to speak because I had the discussion with Mr. Robinson last night after court in connection with this very matter, although in the presence of Ms. Edgerton, and the point I raised with him was that his concern seemed to be provenance. We had encountered that issue during the course of this case countless times, that is, is there an issue about the provenance of the document or not? In many instances, the nature of a particular document precluded such an inquiry or obviated the need for such an inquiry. Sometimes the nature of the document required someone, either the Defence or the Prosecution, to go back to their sources and identify the provenance so that the other party could be satisfied. And we did that on an informal basis, that is, neither party required the other to call a witness to demonstrate the provenance in a classical fashion by adducing evidence from the witness-stand. That has been the practice of the case. So when I discussed that with Mr. Robinson last night, it was based on that practice. And he agreed - as I anticipated - that should we be able to satisfy him as to the provenance that we would proceed in the fashion that has become the practice of this case from the outset, that is, that the document would then be admitted in -- as -- because it -- the authenticity was no longer at issue and it was what it purported to be. So that's the basis for the information that Ms. Edgerton provided today. It is not a -- it's not a case of a -- one of the attorneys testifying in lieu of a witness; it is pursuant to a practice that has been well established in the course of this case and that was confirmed last night during our discussions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: So the provenance is not an issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I -- it should not -- it certainly should not be. We confirmed that. Those representations in the past have been sufficient. Mr. Robinson is certainly welcome to talk to our investigator. I don't think he doubts it and I don't think it is an issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tieger. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, may I caution about a certain matter before you rule? "Sniper position" is the caption and there is no foundation for that. The witness did not confirm this. This was not put to him and the zoom makes it possible to manipulate these photographs easily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow the "sniper position"?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The caption, the caption. It hasn't been interpreted. The caption if you look at this photograph is "sniper position." On the basis of what may this be the caption? It is the description.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Caption or title is not a part of evidence at all. Given the circumstances, in particular that the provenance of the photo is not at issue, the Chamber will receive it. Shall we give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 24121 receives number P6021, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we could just have finally a look at two more photographs in succession, 65 ter number 24135 being the first and 24134 being the second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we have a problem with the e-court?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this photo, Mr. Maletic, is from -- was taken from the 15th floor of Lenjinova Bolnica [phoen] in Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next photograph, please, 24134.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And then I'll have a question for you. And this photo, 65 ter 24134, is a view from the same location at a magnification of 200. In both those photos do you see areas behind the confrontation line as you knew it to be at that time -- as you knew it to be during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what is the question, sorry?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do both these photos depict areas in the enemy territory, in your enemy territory, behind the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot assess that from here. You said that it was seriously magnified. I have to point out that I said in paragraph 25 that civilian zones could be targeted, and as far as I know that did not happen. So as I said, from some positions civilian zones could be targeted but it did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we go back, please, to 65 ter number 24135.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Maletic, you said yesterday that you grew up in Sarajevo and you knew these areas. Do you see here locations behind the enemy's front line?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see those locations here but they're awfully magnified here so I cannot assess where this is viewed from.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, these would be the last two photographs I'd like to have tendered, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we'll stick with our objection, but I just want to - so that we're all on the same page here - understand that these photographs can be admitted to understand the witness's testimony. But as to the representation as to where they're taken from, you don't have any evidence of that and so I take it that that will not be part of the evidence in the case in light if the Prosecution wants to prove where they're taken from, they would call a witness or seek permission to call a witness for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the Chamber is of the view Mr. Robinson's comment is fair enough and in light of the development the Chamber also will reconsider yesterday's decision not to admit 65 ter 23643 and we'll admit the three photos all together. Shall we give the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Photo 24135 receives number P6022. 24134 receives number P6023, and 2463 -- 2463 -- 643 [sic] receives number P6024, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Maletic, you also said in your statement that your Supreme Command regularly informed you of actions that were prohibited because they were contrary to the rules of war, and I wonder did they warn you against the use of prisoners for forced labour in dangerous conditions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was aware of some of these things, but I'm not aware of all the details. We used prisoners at certain moments, like in workshops and things like that. I cannot recall exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's have a look, please, at P5987. It's a document dated 21 May 1993 that you drafted to the command of the 2nd Battalion, reporting on the escape of Muslim prisoners who had been taken from Kula to do labour on the front line. Do you see the document on the page in front of you or on the screen in front of you, rather?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this document says that the prisoners were working under the guard of Zeljko Mitrovic, who you agreed yesterday was in charge of the labour squad in the 2nd Battalion. And when it was found that they escaped, Mitrovic and the two soldiers with him opened fire after the prisoners. Now, would you agree with me, Mr. Maletic, that this is contrary to the rules of war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, there's one thing with regard to this remark. You see, it says here that this took place during the night because this location is exposed to fire all the time. So see, we did make an effort to protect these prisoners because it is impossible to carry out this kind of work during the day. This is a properly drafted note in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that opening fire on prisoners of war is contrary to the rules of war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if they were not running away, fire would not have been opened; however, they formally fired when time had already gone by. You see that in this statement here. So see, they came to inform that and then they only fired formally and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I'm not sure that I understand what "formally firing" means, so let's get back to brass tacks. Would you agree that opening fire on prisoners of war is contrary to the rules of war?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. It seems to me that this question is ambiguous, that the question ought to be whether opening fire on prisoners who are escaping is contrary to the rules of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see much difference. Would you agree that opening fire on prisoners of war is contrary to the rules of war? That was the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Right, but the document indicates that the prisoners were escaping, so that's a totally different situation. In my opinion, maybe I'm wrong, but opening fire on people who are escaping is permissible even in the civilian context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine. We can move on actually. But still on the same theme, did your Supreme Command, when they told you about actions that were prohibited because they were contrary to the rules of war, warn you about forced expulsions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Natural expulsions? Forced expulsions of the population? What was that? I didn't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When your Supreme Command told you about actions that were prohibited because they were contrary to the rules of war, did they tell you that forced expulsions were prohibited?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, what do you mean by "Supreme Command"?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I was taking the wording of -- from the witness's statement, Your Honours, and I'll just give you the paragraph citation in one moment, if I may. Your indulgence for a moment because there's a couple of copies I have of the witness's statement and I'll have to find it. I misspoke, Your Honours, and I find the words of the witness at paragraph 18 and the witness actually said "our superior command regularly informed us." So my apologies. Indeed, I did misspeak.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To go back to the question, Mr. Witness, did your superior command tell you that forced expulsions were prohibited?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can we have a look, please, at P1266. It's a document dated 30 September 1992 which should be available in your language. Thank you. A document dated 30 September 1992 on -- which on B/C/S page 2, the ninth line down, reports on the expulsion of 30 Muslim -- pardon me, 300 Muslim civilians from Grbavica on that day. So despite being warned that forced expulsions were prohibited, Mr. Maletic, in fact, expulsions did take place; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you disputing, Mr. Maletic, the accuracy of this report?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One cannot see from here that they were expelled.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The document specifically states, Mr. Maletic, that the writer was able to confirm that approximately 300 Muslims, Muslim civilians, have been expelled by the Serbs during the day from the area of Grbavica, 150 of them gathered at the Bristol Hotel, and the remaining at Bosnian Assembly building approximately 1 kilometre east from the hotel. And is the fact that they were expelled not obvious from the document on its face, Mr. Maletic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They probably wished to move to the other side of their own accord.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, can the witness be read about the fact that this was found out from the Bosnian liaison officer who was the source of this information?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I haven't read this document. Does it appear on this text, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The sentence reads - and I'm happy to repeat it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: "Through the Bosnian liaison officer the writer was able to confirm that approximately 300 Muslim civilians have been expelled by the Serbs during the day from the area of Grbavica, 150 of them gathered at the Bristol Hotel, and the remaining at the Assembly building of Bosnia and Herzegovina located at approximately 1 kilometre east from the hotel." May I move on, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you just said, Mr. Maletic, that they may have wished to move from Grbavica of their own accord, and on that note perhaps we could look at some of the conditions of life inside Grbavica. I'd like us to go to P1474, and that's the notebook of Dr. -- pardon me, of General Ratko Mladic in which on 25 March 1993 -- pardon me - he had a meeting with Prime Minister Radomir Lukic which referred to, among other things, the situation in Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if we could go to pages 157 of the English transcript and page 159 of the B/C/S original.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On the English page they -- we see where the citation begins. And if we could in both versions go over to the next page. There General Mladic notes: "Some soldiers rape even Serbian women (in Grbavica). (Lukic) himself took someone who had done this out of Sarajevo (he wouldn't say his name)." Does that reflect the conditions of life inside VRS-held Grbavica, Mr. Maletic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this relates to Grbavica, but I don't see what the point was. This was within the remit of the civilian police; however, what was really happening I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, when your superior command told you about certain things that were prohibited, did they tell you that sexual violence was prohibited?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, none of my soldiers was involved in any of such activities; therefore, I have no knowledge about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But nevertheless, despite the warning General Mladic appears to have been informed that it was still going on.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what is the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Despite the warning, it was still going on, don't you agree?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So is it your assertion that General Mladic is ill-informed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only speak about my part of the territory, i.e., the part of Grbavica that was under my control. There were other battalions in the area, for example, an armoured battalion, and so on and so forth. Therefore, I couldn't know everything that was happening among the soldiers. But as far as I know, there were no rapes, not only of Serbian women mentioned here specifically, but of any women at all -- or at least I know nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you were the assistant commander for security and intelligence for your battalion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But you received no information to that effect? You knew nothing about these allegations that even Serbian women were being raped in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you were advised by your superior command about actions that were -- should be prohibited, did they tell you that looting was prohibited?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But yet looting and crime in Grbavica, it seems, were rampant, Mr. Maletic. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you consider a crime if a Serb left Sarajevo, found shelter in a flat or brought his own furniture to an empty flat, do you consider that to be a war crime?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's have a look at P1482, which is another copy of General Mladic's notebook. E-court page 79 in English and page 77 in B/C/S. And it refers to a Supreme Command session of 21 January 1993. And there the defence minister at the time, General Kovacevic, noted the looting and crime in Grbavica and he said of General Dragomir Milosevic: "He did not cope well" -- oh, I'm sorry, I should wait -- thank you. He said of General Dragomir Milosevic: "He did not cope well at Grbavica because he did not prevent the looting and crime." Does this not reflect, Mr. Maletic, that looting and crime was taking place in Grbavica but it was not being prevented by the military command?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, the depth of the Grbavica territory was covered by the civilian police, that is to say the civilian police was in charge of what was happening inside the territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You've actually not answered my question. Mr. Maletic, my question was: Does this notation in General Mladic's diary not reflect that looting and crime was taking place in Grbavica but it was not being prevented by the military command?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as military is concerned, looting was prohibited and I told you what was going on with the soldiers who occupied flats and so on and so forth. As for the looting, we were deployed along the front line so we did not know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if I may, Your Honours, I have two areas that I hope will be rather brief before I conclude.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Maletic, now to go just back briefly to your evidence about snipers in the battalion command, you said - although you were assistant commander for security and intelligence - that you didn't know about the type of assignments and the manner in which they were executed in the case of these snipers. Now, Mr. Maletic, this Chamber has heard evidence that UNPROFOR knew with specialised troops in reconnaissance and surveillance capabilities about the potential sniper positions, they'd photographed them, they'd drawn out all the potential areas, and the reference to that is General Fraser's evidence at transcript pages 8016 to 8017. They were -- they've also heard that UNPROFOR was very familiar with the sniper positions, all for the purpose of having shooters reply to these snipers to protect the civilian. And they've also heard at transcript page 13197 that civilian residents of Grbavica knew not only about the snipers, they knew their names, who they were, and where they operated. So, Mr. Maletic, yesterday you gave evidence that even though you attended briefing meetings at battalion command, both as a company commander and as assistant commander of security and intelligence, and you conceded at page 80 of yesterday's transcript that you received general information about the security situation, I wonder how you can maintain that the civilians in Grbavica and UNPROFOR were actually better informed than you about the names of the snipers in the 2nd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I did not remember their names and I can only repeat that today.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in your statement you also said that you personally saw freedom of movement as something very positive. I'd like us to have a look at another document you wrote, 65 ter number 24156, please. And it's dated 16 May 1993. And I'll just wait until it appears on the screen. To all units of the 2nd Battalion, telling them to fully control and identify persons in their areas of responsibilities and find out their reasons to be there and saying that in case they do not possess approval or a justified reason for that, it's necessary to arrest them immediately and bring them to the battalion command. And if they try to escape, they should be stopped; and if that's not possible, they should be killed. Now, paragraph -- if we could scroll down in English, please. Paragraph 2 of this document and over onto the next page in English, please. Thank you. Paragraph 2 of this document indicates that you've received information from the Croatian Roman Catholic Church that -- or information that the Croatian Roman Catholic Church has engaged some foreign journalists to provide them with TV and photo material on destroyed religious buildings in the area under Muslim control and in the areas of Republika Srpska, and you write that: "In order to prevent such activities, it's necessary to prevent the entrance of foreign journalists to your areas of responsibility, unless they have been previously announced and escorted by the authorised commander from the battalion command." And you also say if these persons are found in your area without an authorisation, their documents and equipment should be confiscated and the battalion command should be contacted for further instruction. So my question to you is: Does this document reflect personal support on your part for freedom of movement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as this document is concerned, it is possible to allow this during the war, since there was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down and speak more intelligibly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreters were not able to hear you because you spoke a bit too fast. Could you repeat your answer slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If such cases did happen, it is possible that this is permissible in war. Since there was no possibility for escape, there were no executions consequently. Therefore, this allegation is groundless. Since this condition was not fulfilled, this kind of caution is justifiable during the war, and I am talking about the front line, the forward line.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could this be marked as a Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 24156 receives number P6025, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I did note that your time was up a while ago, but I take it you will be concluding very soon?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. I think I could -- I think the remaining examination would take - depending on the witness's answers of course - ten minutes, if I may, Your Honours. I'm in Your Honour's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's have -- on the same subject let's have another look at or a look at another document, 65 ter number 24155.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it's a document you wrote on 6 March 1993, indicating that there were three foreign journalists on RS territory and ordering the 4th Company to increase control within their area of responsibility and if they find these journalists to deprive them of freedom of movement and bring them to the battalion command regardless of possible documents that give them permission to work on RS territory. Now, does this document support or reflect your personal support for freedom of movement, as you indicated in your statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This refers only to individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So even though, Mr. Maletic, you indicated personal support for freedom of movement, is your evidence now that that personal support did not apply to individuals, civilians, as is the case in this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see exactly that it says here those who displayed open hatred towards the Serbs and intolerance by means of writing reports, reporting, and thereby caused unimaginable damage to the Serbian people on the international scene. This is what refers to such people.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it was your determination that these journalists who, in your view, were intolerant, it was your determination that these journalists should not have freedom of movement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot allow the enemy to come to my front line and shoot and photograph my positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Maletic, what then makes Tony Ashby, a photographer from Western Australia; Dick Verkijk, a journalist from Holland; and Maxe Tharton, a journalist from Western Australia, the enemy?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information that we received from the command, one can see exactly from this document what this is all about. That means that these journalists are allowed to move around but they are prohibited from coming to the front line in order to prevent them from photographing the positions that could possibly be then shelled the following day.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could this be a Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 24155 receives number P6026, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now one last question. You talked in your statement about Veselin Vlahovic and Zoran Vitkovic in the area of Grbavica and you said you were not aware of the entire spectrum of problems these paramilitary units were causing. But, Mr. Maletic, Colonel Osmic, as he was at the time, advised General Mladic on 16 June 1992 - and the reference is P1478, pages 172, 173, in English; and 170, 171 in B/C/S - Colonel Milosevic told General Mladic Zoran Vitkovic is the chief of those who steal. And that's the same Zoran Vitkovic that you referred to in your statement, isn't it, Mr. Maletic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I spoke about Zoran Vitkovic and I said that since at the time I was a soldier I only know - and I included that in my statement - that there was a group under the command of Zoran Vitkovic and they were headquartered in the building --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the name of the building.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They used to go to certain sections of the front line where the Serbian fighters needed assistance because they were under enemy attack. During one such attack by the Muslim forces, Zoran Vitkovic got killed --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Maletic, Mr. Maletic, you answered my question with the first two words in your sentence which is "yes. Yes." So I'd like to move on. Now, this Chamber has also heard evidence from Mr. Ratomir Neskovic who was formerly president of the Crisis Staff for Novo Sarajevo about the other man you referred to, Veselin Vlahovic, Batko, in other words, and at T 14315 to 14316 Dr. Karadzic referred Mr. Neskovic to his previous testimony in the Krajisnik case about Batkovic, and Mr. Neskovic said -- and here's what was spoken about in the Krajisnik case. Mr. Neskovic in that case said -- was asked: "Was it understood that the primary targets of his attacks were Muslims and Croats?" And his answer was: "To some extent, yes, but the main targets of his attacks always had to do with money and looting and then of course especially Muslims and Croats, mostly Muslims." So, Mr. Maletic, president of the Crisis Staff for Novo Sarajevo knew about the spectrum of crimes that Batko was involved in. Colonel Milosevic and General Mladic also knew. So how can you, a man who grew up in Sarajevo, a company commander on the front line in Sarajevo, assistant commander for intelligence and security for your battalion, claim - whose job it was to collect information - how can you claim that you didn't know of the spectrum of crimes that these individuals committed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That man disappeared from the area before I joined the command as company commander and assistant commander for intelligence and security.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Nothing further, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Maletic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have P998 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the document, in paragraph 18 of your statement you said that the superior commands advised you of any prohibition to take action, and Ms. Edgerton asked you something about that. I would like you to have a look at the document. I would like to see the last page of the document if possible. In the English the penultimate page, please. Can you see who this was sent to and did your unit also receive these instructions for further action?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll read out the last sentence of paragraph 6. "It is most stringently forbidden to mistreat civilian unarmed population and treat the prisoners in keeping with the Geneva Conventions." Did you receive this? Is this what you had in mind? And did you abide by these instructions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received these instructions and we abided by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go back to P6025 again. P6025. It was admitted just earlier today. I wanted to focus on paragraph 1 which esteemed Madam Edgerton failed to read. Could you please read it out aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "We received information from several sources that groups of American special forces (members of the so-called 'Green Berets,' target scouts - road scouts) have already been inserted into the territory of the former BiH. In the event of foreign military intervention, they are supposed to execute tasks such as guiding the air force, securing airborne landing areas, collecting data on strength of Serbian units, identifying and selecting the targets for air-strikes, and other special assignments."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was the prohibition referred to in paragraph 1 supposed to be referring to -- sorry, item 4 -- no, sorry. Actually, the last paragraph of paragraph 1, "with the aim of discovering," et cetera. Who did this refer to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The American special forces, and that is why I issued this order, or rather, piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So members of the aforementioned groups?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says groups of American special forces that have been inserted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you read this aloud, "in case there is no ..." et cetera.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The last paragraph of item 1.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "With the aim of detecting ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, the sentence after that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now it's gone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please wait for page 2 because the interpreters cannot see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you read slowly again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the English translation be placed on the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Unless there are solid grounds and justification, arrest immediately and bring to battalion command. If they try to flee, prevent them from doing so. If that is impossible, liquidate them."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How would you or how did you treat the Serbs who moved about the lines unauthorised? Did you apply measures against them as well?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. No unauthorised access was allowed to the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 3 of item 3.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we have that on the screen, please, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "If such persons are encountered in the combat area ...," et cetera. What is the key point here? What dictates your treatment of such people? In other words, what was happening with those who were authorised access?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they had authorised access, they could continue filming and go about their journalistic tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked about this alleged expulsion. While you were there, were there exchanges taking place organised by commissions in keeping with certain lists; and if so, where, at what bridges did such occurrences take place?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Before the witness answers, that's -- perhaps we could ask Dr. Karadzic to rephrase because that's a very leading question or perhaps it's been so leading that maybe there's no point in him rephrasing any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise. It is the habit I have since the Prosecution case. It seems to be difficult to be rid of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maletic, what was happening with the people who wanted to cross from one side to the other? How was that regulated?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have mentioned here that for a while the blue routes were open and they were free to cross the bridges both ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could anyone go as they pleased or was it regulated?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the prior agreement of the warring parties and provided there was a truce, a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now have P6019. Could you tell us, what is the green building across the street, if you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps it's the building next to the machine engineering school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was stated that this picture was taken from the 6th floor or the roof of the Lenjinova Street building. Did you have sniper positions on the 6th -- sorry, the 13th floor of that building in Lenjinova Street or perhaps on the roof?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the front line and the fighters were dug in at the foot of the buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 6020 next.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As for the previous question, can you say yes or no? Did you have sniper positions at that height?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have sharpshooters in my unit. As for this photograph, this picture was taken after the war, that's what we were told, so this is not accurate. Perhaps there was a tree here. Another thing, it is incomprehensible that traffic was allowed on the Muslim side when they initiated combat, thus exposing vehicles and civilians to danger. There was a real danger of being hit by stray bullets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Maletic, what did you mean by saying that you "did not have sharpshooters in my unit"? Did you mean that there was no sniper in that position or you didn't have snipers at all in your unit?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please receive the following interpretation: Sharpshooters or snipers -- could the witness receive accurate interpretation in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So could you clarify what you meant by saying: "I did not have sharpshooters in my unit"?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said "snajperisti" and it was interpreted as "sharpshooter."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Sharpshooter and sniper are interchangeable terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are not giving evidence, Mr. Karadzic. I was asking Mr. Maletic. Did you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. While I commanded the company in 1992 or part of that year, in our company we did not have sniper shooters. Our defence line was at the foot of the buildings. We had semi-automatic and automatic rifles, machine-guns, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is the date of the document of the list of names we saw yesterday, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The list is undated, Your Honours. It includes the name of one Aco Petrovic who the witness said replaced the previous battalion commander at a particular date which I can find momentarily. So it's safe to assume that the list does not date from 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all due respect for the interpreters, I wanted to ask you this: Is "strelac" and "snajperisti" the same thing?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: In the Serbian, there is a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you, Mr. Maletic. "Sharpshooter was being interpreted to you as "strelac." Are there words as "strelac" and "snajperisti" in military parlance? Is there a difference?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Snajperisti" is a sniper shooter. Perhaps the other term applied to a soldier with an automatic rifle. That's what we call "strelac."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 6022.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have positions at or on the 15th floor of Lenjinova Street or on the roof? Did you have positions there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our positions were at the foot of the buildings there and we had fortified dug-outs and bunkers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A hypothetical question, if I may, as a soldier could you tell us what would be the trajectory of a projectile which went through a tram, a streetcar, what would the trajectory look like? Where would be the exit and the entry point?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What it would look like --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Before the witness answers, I would submit that doesn't arise from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You showed this picture and he's putting his question based upon this picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I understand Your Honour's ruling then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If one were to shoot from this height, from the 15th floor or the roof of the high-rise on the tram tracks, what would be the height of the entry and exit hole? Would there be a difference?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There would be a drastic difference. The entry point would go perhaps through the roof or the top of the tram and the lower part would go further below.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 2126 and I would kindly ask the usher to hand the pen to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maletic, can you identify this? Where was this photograph taken from, from which position?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot find my way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see Metaljka over there in the background?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you mark the faculty of philosophy and the museum?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The national museum, Zemaljski Muse?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How shall I mark it? Should I put a circle there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you put number 1 by the museum.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the building and the yard, does that also belong to the museum?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please mark the faculty of philosophy.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, please, do you see the river-bed, on that side, the Serb side, can you mark your positions? Can you mark your positions by drawing a red line.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any positions on the buildings up there? For example, on the 7th floor of Metaljka, did you have a position there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. These ones mentioned at Metaljka 1 and 2, we used them only at night because we could not approach them during the day. So we used them mostly at night. All the positions were at lower levels of the buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us this, these positions at lower levels -- actually, where were their positions? Can you use the green marker or some other colour to mark their positions facing you? Well, the green one wouldn't be readily visible. Take any colour, blue will do.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were they just by the river or a bit further off?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were in these buildings at lower levels and in certain areas we saw that they were right by the river underneath that concrete there. So it's at lower levels by the buildings, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there anything on these buildings, the museum, was there anything there by way of military installations? Were they used?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So your positions were dug in and could you see beyond their lines? Could you have a clear line of sight? You refer to this in your statement. Is that what you meant when you said that from your positions you could not see them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I tried to say, that you could not see the depth of the territory from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that opposite the faculty there is S, or rather, this is a line where the tram moves onto the other side of the street. So you can only see the beginning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you're leading in a --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know of some curve where the tram had to slow down?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did your soldiers await an opportunity there to fire at the tram?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was always prohibited, to fire at civilians in civilian targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether you see that red building in the background, can you indicate who kept what under their control behind Metaljka and can you draw that for us?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not the line of my battalion. I just know that in this red building -- well, it was partly Serb positions and partly Muslim positions in that red building. This was not the area of responsibility of my battalion so I just heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you put a circle around that building that had been divided between the two armies?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise, but I think it is this building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. By the trenches -- actually, could you put number 4 by this building and could you mark the trenches by 3.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 3? Our trenches, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You can also place number 4 by this red building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the Chamber needs to rise at 10.30 sharp, so if you need more time we'll break now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no, Excellencies. I could finish now but I would like to ask Mr. Maletic to place a date here and to initial this photograph and could it please be admitted, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be next Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be document number D2525, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, would it be wise to have the clean underlying photograph also admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see any problem. That will be Exhibit D2526.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Just an observation, Dr. Karadzic, if you ask someone if they agree with some proposition which you then make, that is always a leading question, and that's what you tend to do. It's something you drum into law students not to do. You'll find if you preface your questions with: What, when, who, or where, well that doesn't always exclude a leading question; it helps to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. You are right. I'm aware of this habit of mine, if you will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you done with your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellencies. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Mr. Maletic, that concludes your evidence. Please have a safe journey back home. We'll rise all together and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will give its oral rulings on three matters. First the Chamber will issue an oral ruling on the accused's motion to vary list of witnesses filed confidentially -- I'm sorry, filed publicly with confidential annexes on the 22nd of November, 2012. In the motion the accused requests that the Chamber allow him to vary his list of witnesses pursuant to Rule 73 ter (D) by adding one witness. The accused further notifies the Chamber that he does not intend to call an additional batch of 26 witnesses who previously appeared on his witness list. Moreover, the accused informs the Chamber that the witness he seeks to add benefits from Rule 70 conditions from a previous case and thus he attaches the factual basis for his request as well as the witness's proposed statement as confidential annexes A and B to the motion. On the 23rd of November, 2012, the Prosecution filed its response, stating that it does not oppose the accused's motion. Having reviewed the information in annex A to the motion and the proposed statement in annex B for the witness the accused wishes to add to his witness list, and considering that the Prosecution does not oppose this addition, the Chamber finds that there is good cause to allow the accused to add this witness to his list and grants the accused's motion in this respect. With regard to the Rule 70 conditions in place for this witness from a prior case, the Chamber reminds the accused that it is his obligation to make the appropriate Rule 70 application to the Chamber for witnesses he wishes to call. The Chamber further notes that there is no such a thing as an "existing Rule 70 protective measures" that continues from case to case and that the Chamber must decide these issues anew in each case. Accordingly, the Chamber instructs the accused to file a Rule 70 application for this witness, attaching all relevant correspondence with the state requesting the Rule 70 conditions well in advance of the witness's scheduled testimony. Accordingly, the Chamber grants the motion and allows the accused to add the witness named in confidential annex A to the motion to his 65 ter list. The Chamber will now issue its ruling on the Prosecution's request, made orally on the 28th of November 2012, that the accused be ordered to provide the Prosecution with outstanding witness statements for all the witnesses he intends to call during his defence case. In terms of dead-line, the Prosecution requests that the accused be ordered to disclose these statements by the end of December insofar as witnesses related to the municipalities and hostages components of the case are concerned and by the end of January in relation to Srebrenica witnesses. In support, the Prosecution argues that the accused has failed to comply with Rule 65 ter (G) of the Tribunal's Rules in that his list of witnesses does not contain adequate factual summaries of the witnesses' evidence. Since the Prosecution has also not been provided with witness statements for many of the witnesses, it is unable to undertake investigations relating to those witnesses or identify the extent to which they contradict each other. The Prosecution also submits that, as instructed by the Chamber during the pre-Defence conference, it tried to find a solution with the Defence without the Chamber's involvement. However, it was advised by the Defence team that further information on the witnesses' evidence would not be forthcoming due to the Defence's lack of time and resources. In that respect, the Prosecution notes that the accused has been warned by the Chamber that his witness list is excessive and includes a large number of witnesses who are to provide irrelevant, marginal, or manifestly repetitive information, which in turn contributes to the time and resource obstacles faced by the Defence. The Prosecution finally explains that in asking for witness statements rather than adequate Rule 65 ter factual summaries, it is trying to alleviate the Defence's workload as the summaries can only be provided after the statements have been drawn up. In response, the accused submits that he opposes the request as it is impossible for the Defence to meet the dead-lines requested without more time and resources. The accused's legal advisor, Mr. Robinson, adds that the Defence team has done everything possible to provide as much information as possible to the Prosecution concerning Defence witnesses, which included disclosing some 160 witness statements so far. He reiterates, however, that the Defence does not have the resources to take all the statements by December and January. As for providing more detailed summaries of the evidence, Mr. Robinson submits that this would amount to speculation since the Defence does not have more information in relation to witnesses who have not yet been interviewed. Accordingly, Mr. Robinson concludes that it would be best for the Prosecution and the Defence to continue working together as they have done until now. In cases where the Prosecution is disadvantaged by late notice, the Chamber can postpone the testimony of affected witnesses. The Chamber has reviewed the Rule 65 ter summaries provided by the accused and agrees with the Prosecution that a significant number of those summaries do not provide adequate notice regarding the witnesses' evidence. For example, for many of the witnesses, the summaries are general in nature and provide very little information other than the component of the case to which the witness is relevant. In addition, many are formulaic with the same summary being provided over and over again, with very little or no difference between the witnesses. Furthermore, as recently submitted by Mr. Robinson, the list also does not include the witnesses whose evidence has been admitted or is sought for admission pursuant to Rules 92 bis and 92 quater, despite Rule 65 ter (G) clearly implying that those witnesses should be included too. Accordingly, the Chamber is of the view that the accused's witness list, as it stands now, is not in compliance with Rule 65 ter (G). The Chamber does accept that the accused and his team are working hard to obtain the witness statements of all the witnesses on the accused's revised witnesses list of 11th of September, 2012. However, the Chamber also notes that that list contains 583 witnesses who are to testify under Rule 92 ter, with the exception of the accused himself, and yet the Defence is in possession of only around 160 witness statements so far. The implication is, therefore, that around 420 witnesses have not been interviewed by the Defence at this stage. It is also clear from the submission made before the Chamber that a large number of these witnesses have never been contacted by the Defence and probably do not even know that they are on the accused's witness list. This is an extremely unsatisfactory state of affairs at this stage of the trial and is not conducive to its efficiency. The Chamber recalls here that it has already warned the accused during the Status Conference of 3rd of September, 2012, that the first version of his witness list which contained 579 witnesses was causing concern as it, among other things, included a large number of witnesses whose evidence was completely or largely irrelevant to the charges in the indictment as well as unnecessarily repetitive witnesses. The Chamber even provided specific examples of such witnesses and then ordered the accused to revise the witness list, bearing in mind all those concerns. When the accused eventually filed a revised witness list on the 11th of September, 2012, he dropped only ten witnesses and included a number of character witnesses with the result that the total number of witnesses currently listed on the 65 ter list is 583. Since then, several witnesses have been dropped by the Defence due to their refusal to come and give evidence and the accused has removed an additional 20-odd witnesses as indicated by my earlier oral ruling. The Chamber is in agreement with the Prosecution that the accused's problem with providing adequate factual summaries for his witness list stems from his failure to adequately revise what is a very unrealistic and excessive witness list. The Chamber is also concerned because it seems that the accused's witness list was compiled without the accused and his Defence team knowing what the listed witnesses will in fact testify about. This is not only unfair to the Prosecution but also goes against the spirit of the Rules and causes the Chamber to question the accused's ability to adequately represent himself and organise his Defence case properly. As the accused must be aware, the Chamber has to ensure that this trial is fair both to him and to the Prosecution. The Chamber is also under the obligation to make sure that the trial is expeditious, which means that the accused cannot be allowed to call an unnecessarily large number of witnesses, especially if their evidence is also irrelevant or only marginally relevant to the charges against him or if they are unnecessarily repetitive. For all those reasons, the Chamber has come to the conclusion that the Prosecution's request should be granted in part. The Chamber therefore orders the accused to provide the Prosecution with adequate summaries under Rule 65 ter of the evidence of all the witnesses he intends to call. He shall do so by the end of January 2013 in relation to the witnesses dealing with the municipalities and hostages components of the case, and by the end of February 2013 in relation to the Srebrenica component of the case. Given the Chamber's guide-lines on the conduct of this trial of 8th of October, 2009, it shall not order the accused to provide witness statements to the Prosecution by those dates, but rather leaves that option open to the parties to agree on should it be more practicable. While the accused and Mr. Robinson have submitted that the provision of the summaries by the dead-lines sought by the Prosecution will be an impossible task, the Chamber recalls its position that the accused's witness list, even in its current revised form, is unrealistic and unreasonable for all the reasons outlined during the Status Conference of the 3rd of September. Accordingly, the Chamber orders the accused to further revise his witness list by Friday, 14th of December, 2012, and, in doing so, to make a serious attempt at including only those witnesses who are to give evidence relevant to the charges in the indictment and who are not unnecessarily repetitive. Furthermore, in order to comply with Rule 65 ter (G), the accused shall include all Rule 92 bis and Rule 92 quater witnesses whose evidence was sought for admission prior to 27th of August, 2012, and the admission of which has been granted by the Chamber, as well as Krnojelac whose Rule 92 quater evidence is currently being considered for admission by the Chamber. Once the list is revised as instructed, the task of providing the summaries by January and February will be less daunting. The Chamber finally notes that if, following the filing of the revised witness list, it is not satisfied that the accused has made a genuine attempt to focus on relevant witnesses alone, it will consider imposing, pursuant to Rule 73 ter (C), a limit on the number of witnesses he may call. Finally, the Chamber recalls that the accused's motion for clarification of decision on Defence witness interviews, dated 26th of November, 2012, is still pending. Given that the issues raised therein, and particularly the number of witnesses the Prosecution wishes to interview, are linked to the accused's witness list, the Chamber shall postpone its decision on that motion until the revised witness list is filed by the accused and the Prosecution is able to revise the list of witnesses it wishes to interview. In that respect, the Prosecution shall, by Friday, 21st of December, 2012, inform the Chamber whether the number of witnesses it wishes to interview has changed and, if so, shall notify the accused and the VWS of the new list of those witnesses. The Chamber shall then proceed to issue its decision on the accused's motion for clarification of decision on Defence witness interviews. Finally, the Chamber will issue an oral ruling on the Prosecution's motion to exclude the evidence in part of witness Milan Pejic filed on 30th of November, 2012, wherein the Prosecution seeks the partial exclusion of Milan Pejic's evidence on the basis that some parts are irrelevant to the charges in the indictment and the accused's responsibility. The accused filed his response on the 3rd of December, 2012, opposing the motion and contending that the material is, indeed, relevant to his case. The Chamber reminds the accused, once again, that it will not admit tu quoque evidence under the guise of relevance to this trial. Accordingly, the Chamber orders that the third subparagraph of paragraph 24 should be excluded from the witness's statement as well as paragraph 27 and the four documents referred to in the second subparagraph of paragraph 24. Further, while the Chamber considers that the remainder of the witness's statement is of some relevance to the indictment, it finds paragraph 17 difficult to understand and would benefit from the witness's live explanation on this paragraph. The Chamber therefore grants the motion in part, excludes the third subparagraph of paragraph 24 as well as paragraph 27 and the four documents referred to in the second subparagraph of paragraph 24, and allows the accused to tender the remainder of Milan Pejic's statement pursuant to Rule 92 ter. It further orders that the accused seek further explanation on the evidence in paragraph 17 live from the witness. Finally, the Chamber orders that the Prosecution shall have 30 minutes for its cross-examination. Unless there are any other matters, we'll bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like now to read the summary of Mr. Blasko Rasevic's statement in English. [In English] Blasko Rasevic lived in Sarajevo. He was a bus driver at GSP, city public transport, in Sarajevo. At some point in the winter of 1991 and 1992 and from then on, his colleagues and he observed a group of men with automatic rifles and dressed in camouflage uniforms which he had not seen until then. The uniforms were neither of the police nor of the JNA and they also wore green berets. These groups were the Green Berets and the Patriotic League, formed by the leaders of the SDA. He and his colleagues on other bus lines were stopped by these groups who then searched them, the passengers, and the buses. Bus searches were often conducted in an arrogant manner, with open hostility towards the Serbs. It was rumoured and eventually confirmed that the members of these formations were Muslims from the criminal circles. In late January or early February 1992, these armed paramilitary groups started to move freely during the day. Serbs then in beginning of March 1992 set up barricade in the area of the city where they had been the majority in order to protect themselves and their families. At the same time, Muslims erected their barricades in the areas where they have constituted the majority. The barricades were in place until the 3rd of March, 1992, when the three peoples made a political agreement to form mixed patrols which were operational until April when the Muslims perfidiously killed Serb police officer Pero Petrovic. Blasko Rasevic states with full responsibility that the Serbs were deceived by the Muslims into accepting these joint patrols and the removal of the original barricades. The patrols were active, but the armed groups, the Green Berets and the Patriotic League, continued to operate alongside these patrols and exclusively at night. Therefore, the barricades were removed but armed men remained and exercised control on the quiet. When the Serbs lifted their barricades and took part in the joint patrols, the Muslim forces took the opportunity, with support of the MUP, police, to put under their control parts of the city that had previously been under Serb control, like Pofalici, Buca Potok, Pionirska Dolina, and others. On 4 April 1992 he was stopped by members of the Green Berets and the Patriotic League and searched once again. That day, fearing for his life, he decided to no longer go to work until the situation normalised. That same day, realising that they were in the part of the city where Muslims were controlling, dominant, he and his family fled to Mrkovici. In Mrkovici, the police had openly sided with the Muslims and the JNA had no power whatsoever. The neighbours assembled in the village school and decided to self-organise in order to protect themselves. They formed the two platoons comprised of volunteering civilians and ten reserve policemen from the Mrkovici local commune. He was in charge of one of those platoons. On 5th of April, 1992, a group of Serbian refugees from the area of Pionirska Dolina and the surrounding villages fled to Mrkovici, seeking refuge. They managed to provide shelter and food for some of those people and because there were many of them they sent the others towards the Romanija plateau. At dusk, the two platoons set off and took up positions at Velika-Tvrdjava-Spicaste-Stijene elevation. They held that line successfully until the end of the war. When the VRS was formed on the 12th of May, 1992, his platoon became part of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade. From their positions they could observe the Muslim artillery firing positions in the city, situated in civilian facilities. His unit was often targeted by mortars mounted on trailers. Muslim forces repeatedly launched random artillery attacks on the village, damaging a large number of family homes and wounding and killing civilians. Throughout the war his unit only carried out defensive tasks and never received an order to attack. Never he nor any other members of his unit or their subordinated or superior commands intended to cause civilian casualties or terrorise civilians in the territory under Muslim control or exert psychological influence on them. They never received or issued any verbal or written orders to that effect. Muslim forces often violated truce agreements to advance closer to their positions -- to the Serb positions. They later lied to the media that it was Serb forces that were violating the truce. They did this constantly prior to a planned attack, falsely briefing the media that Serb forces were attacking them in a particular area. Blasko Rasevic and his unit used this to their advantage, considering those an indication of when and where the Muslim forces would attack them. 50 per cent of the casualties in his unit were inflicted by the Muslim sniper fire. The opposing unit to his was the 105th Mountain Brigade and another Muslim brigade, which he doesn't remember the name. On June the 8th, 1992, Muslim unit launched a large-scale attack, which they successfully repelled. The bodies of Muslim soldiers remained on the battle-field and the Blasko Rasevic's unit pulled the dead and buried them and then exchanged them, which shows that -- with the full respect of the international law and also it was -- they had been acting in defence and the other side was attacking them. On 29th of January, 1993, Muslim forces launched a strong attack and temporarily took control of Mala Tvrdjava, a small castle. The next day his unit made an unprecedented effort and re-established control over Mala Tvrdjava. In total they had five casualties and 22 wounded soldiers. His unit had a very fair relationship with civilian authorities. Due to the difficult situation and poverty, his unit organised a soup kitchen in the village providing meals for the entire local population as well as that of surrounding villages. Mr. Rasevic's unit never opened fire at civilians in Sedrenik. After the incident that took place in February 1994 in Markale, there was a firm conviction in his unit that the Serb forces had not committed the incident and especially not the forces from Mrkovici because someone would have had to know about it and such information would have certainly leaked in their own unit. [Interpretation] Now, this was the summary.

utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, as you have noted that your evidence in chief in most part was admitted in writing in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Yes, Ms. Iodice.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Rasevic.

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, in paragraph 20 of your statement you say that the Mrkovici company was part of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade. Your brigade commander was Miroslav Krajisnik; right?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC
utterances.text: No, Madam Prosecutor. Miroslav Krajisnik was the commander of the light Kosevo Brigade. When the VRS was established, my company became part of the 2nd Motorised Romanija Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Who was your commander, do you remember?

utterances.text: Yes, I do. The first commander of the 2nd Motorised Romanija Brigade was Lieutenant-Colonel Radislav Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Were you within the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, later on we certainly were. But that was after two or three months, I'm not sure. In any case, then we became part of the 1st Romanija Brigade, which was later part of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And at that point your commander was Vlado Lizdek; right?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC
utterances.text: Before Vlado Lizdek, colonel, the commander of the 1st Romanija Brigade was Colonel Dragomir Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC
