utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Were you a member of the SDS before and during the war?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the SDS when it was established in 1990. I was a member and - how should I put it? - I had no position in the party. I was an ordinary member and I still am -- actually, I'm no longer an active member but I'm a sympathiser of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And as a member and supporter, you were informed of the party's goals and policies; right?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as much as I could, as little time that I had once the war broke out because there was no time afterwards, but I wasn't particularly interested in politics. We were all there, at least the people I associated with. Everyone was concerned because of the whole situation. Muslims talked about Alija and the Serbs talked about their leadership and apparently they couldn't agree on how to resolve the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And you heard about the six strategic goals of the Serbian people; right?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC
utterances.text: One couldn't really say I understood them at the time. I wasn't engaged in all that back then. I'm not certain about that. I really couldn't tell them what they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: You didn't hear that one of the goals was the division of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC
utterances.text: Actually, the Serbian Democratic Party -- or actually, the representatives of Serbs, not only the SDS, at the time proposed a cantonal division in Bosnia and Herzegovina of some sort. As for the division of Sarajevo, once it had all fallen through and the conflict broke out, that option appeared, to divide Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And --

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: -- and although you weren't very much interested in politics, you were elected -- you were appointed as a member of the War Commission for the Serbian municipality of Sarajevo centre; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall that. I never received such document. It may well be that someone somewhere put it in writing, but I really don't know a thing about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Okay. I'll try to refresh your memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: If we can have in e-court 65 ter 24245.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: So this is a presidential order dated 21st of July, 1992, and signed by the accused, Dr. Radovan Karadzic. And you were appointed as one of the five members of the War Commission for the Serbian municipality of Sarajevo centre. Does this refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC
utterances.text: This doesn't tell me anything. At this time, I was way too busy with combat operations so that it would apply -- well, I know all these names. There's no denying that. But this doesn't tell me anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: What this document tells you is that the appointment of the members of the War Commission were confirmed and one of the members was Blasko Rasevic under number 4. You were one of these members, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC
utterances.text: I can see it here on this piece of paper. It is true what I can see, but I'm telling you I have never received it and I have no clue, no idea, really.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: I would ask this document to be admitted, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 24245 becomes Exhibit P2527 [sic], Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise. Exhibit P6027, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: So moving now to a different topic and I want to discuss your role as Mrkovici Company commander. In paragraph 29 of your statement you say that you held this position from the 31st of January, 1993, to September 1994?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And your company didn't have two commanders, right?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, after he was killed -- my commander was Bojo Dragas. He was killed on the 30th of January, 1993, when we recaptured Mala Tvrdjava. I was his deputy at the time. Automatically, I became in charge of the company. It lasted -- well, I can't remember exactly because I got fed up at some point. I was replaced by Sasa Maksimovic. He didn't stay in that position long, only a month or two, and I returned to be the company commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And that was Sinisa Maksimovic, not Sasa Maksimovic; right?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC
utterances.text: Correct, you're right. You're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And that happened -- Mr. Maksimovic came here to testify and he said that he was the company commander from the 27th of July, 1994. So is it correct that you probably left the command at the end of July 1994 -- rather, in September?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't pin-point it, but I believe it was the 4th of September, 1994, when I left, and he was probably in that position until the 27th of July. He was there for only two or three months. He wasn't there long. He was a young guy who had just come out of school. When Spicaste Stijene fell on one occasion, he withdrew from the position and I took over the company until early September 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 23 --

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: -- of your statement, you spoke about being targeted by mortars placed on trailer vehicles and hid them behind buildings, schools, kindergartens, hospitals, and they were firing from these positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: If we could go the English to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: So those mortars that you discussed were hidden within civilian facilities; correct?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And you could not see them since they were hidden; right?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, we saw them when they opened fire at us from those vehicles, from the back of those vehicles. Immediately after firing they would flee, taking cover. As for the mortars, in the yard of the Nemanja Vlatkovic school, which was a school for mentally challenged children -- well, by that time they had emptied the school. Then in the Kosevo Hospital they opened fire from there daily. Those working in the Kosevo Hospital told me later that they came there as well with trucks where the mortars were. They would fire and flee. Kosevo was in open view.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And you anticipated one of my next questions. You said that they would fire and then very quickly move. So if you wanted to respond to this fire you had to be very quick, you have to fire immediately, because otherwise they would move and be somewhere else; right?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. In such circumstances when we knew they fired from such positions, we didn't even respond. We didn't want to open random fire. As for their positions where they were deployed, we would get in touch with our superior command of what was going on and then they would make decisions as to whether to engage or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And engaging after they had moved would have had no effect, right, because by then the mortars would have been gone?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you, as for the mortars mounted on vehicles, on the chassises of vehicles or trailers, we couldn't engage them because they would fire one or two up to three shells and move away. There would have been no point and we didn't engage them. As for those we did, when we found out that they fired from different kind of positions, we did engage. We used what we had because the biggest piece we had was a Browning and we could only reach them by that. In that way we would try to make them run.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Didn't your unit also have mortars?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC
utterances.text: No. My company had only 60-millimetre mortars, the small ones, and we had two 84-millimetre pieces later on. That's all we had.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And moving on to the next subject, you agree that from your positions you had a very good view over the city; right?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And is it your evidence that SRK never fired from Spicaste Stijene at all?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC
utterances.text: To my knowledge, never. Now, whether it happened when I was absent - and there isn't much chance of that because I was there non-stop at the lines - in my knowledge they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have in e-court Exhibit P1619. This is a report dated 5th of March, 1995. And if we go to page 3 in English and in B/C/S, we can see under 8(a) (ii) and (iii), we can see that on that day two civilians were wounded from fire coming from Sharpstone, Spicaste Stijene. So if we now go back to page 1 in English and B/C/S, under number 3(b) we can see that after that incident the EgyBat returned the fire on the Bosnian Serb positions at Sharpstone and received a phone call from Radava Battalion commander stating that -- stating that if "the EgyBat APC in his target practice area ... is not removed within 30 minutes it will be fired upon.' Shortly after this call the sector commander arrived at the APC location ... " If we now move to 65 ter 23943 and we go to page 6. It should be the next page probably. Just a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I misspoke. The 65 ter should be 23935. My apologies again. The number is 29935.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise, 29935 is not in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: I will leave it, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic --

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Just for a second, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry, the correct number is 23935. And if we can go to page 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, this document is dated 22nd of August, 1995, and if we go to the bottom of the page at the end it says at -- and I'll read it for you since there's no translation. "At 221425B, 1 X mortar shell and 1 X RPG rocket were fired by BSA soldiers from north-east of Sedrenik ... towards downtown." So do you now agree that Bosnian Serb soldiers in your area were firing at Sedrenik and towards the city and on civilian targets?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC
utterances.text: I don't agree. I mean, we never fired at civilian targets. As for this case, I was no longer at Mrkovici, I mean I had left. So that means that I cannot comment upon this. But I claim that my unit never, absolutely never, opened fire at the civilian population except for where we had observed their machine-gun nests or mortars or -- I mean those launching ferry boats, what they used to target us, but never, never, I am not aware that that happened.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we kindly ask for a clarification here. Where is it written that civilians were fired at? And what does this mean, north-east of Sedrenik?

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: The first document identified two civilians victims, P1619, on page 3. This document identifies firing from north-east of Sedrenik and I can ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: North-east of Sedrenik corresponds more or less to your location; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you couldn't exactly put it that way. We were to the north of Sedrenik. Now, I mean -- well, Sedrenik is sort of a settlement that is wider than Spicaste Stijene, so to the north of Sedrenik and to the north-east, that's where this other hill was and that's where their forces were, opposite us. The altitude is the same like Spicaste Stijene so that would be it. So it's a question of 50 or 100 metres. That's the difference. So then there is Sedam Suma, seven forests, Podrugav Do [phoen], and other locations that they held. It was the other side that held that and that is to the north-east.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, this document identified -- identifies the side that was firing towards down-town. It says from the BSA, which is the acronym for Bosnian Serb army. This fire wasn't coming from the Muslim positions. This fire was coming from the Bosnian Serb side.

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC
utterances.text: It has to do with these two civilians who were killed, right, at Sedrenik? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: No, I'm now talking of this document that you have in front of you. This document says that one mortar shell was fired from the Bosnian Serb side towards down-town.

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I see. So, so, at that time I was no longer at Mrkovici. I was no longer company commander there. I left. I'm looking at the date here. I left. I went from there, so I cannot confirm this, I cannot deny it, because I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And you also cannot exclude that there was firing from the SRK positions at Spicaste Stijene; right?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of this document I cannot. I was not there and I really cannot talk about things I haven't seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask for the admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 23935 receives number P6028, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Just a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, Excellency. So could the same document please be returned now. We can finish before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Rasevic, now I'm going to read the next line to you. I'll read it out in English so that they translate it better than I would. [In English] "At 221430B, 3 X mortar shells were fired from Grdonj ... to Stari Grad ..." [Interpretation] Who held Grdonj?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC
utterances.text: Grdonj was held by the Muslim forces throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was the majority population in Stari Grad?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC
utterances.text: In Stari Grad the majority population was Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And which forces held Stari Grad under their control?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC
utterances.text: Stari Grad was under the control of the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the lines were about 50 metres away. What would be necessary? What kind of proximity would be needed to establish from where the fire came, Serb or Muslim, if they're only 50 metres away from each other?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I mentioned the example of Spicaste Stijene only a moment ago and that other area, Podlugav Brijeg [phoen], we called it that. I don't know what it's really called. That's precisely the case because the altitude is the same to the north, or rather to the north-east. It's the same locations. So it was very hard there to establish where a sniper shot could have come from, if any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rasevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, then that concludes your evidence, Mr. Rasevic. On behalf of the Chamber I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you're free to go. We'll rise --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Excellency. I would also like to thank you for your fairness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll rise all together and we'll have a break for half an hour. I wanted to tell you this before we started today, but given that there's a hearing at 3.00 scheduled to take place in this courtroom, we need to rise at 4.30 and we'll have a -- 2.30, 1430, yes, 2.30, we'll have a shorter break for today. We'll resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, would the witness take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. For this session we are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis with Judge Lattanzi being away due to urgent official matters. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Cvoro.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have in e-court 1D6801.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cvoro, did you give a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: Yes, I gave a statement that we see here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please approach the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Cvoro, could you come closer to the microphone so that the interpreters could hear you better.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you read this statement and sign it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I read the statement and signed the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm waiting for the interpretation and I'm kindly asking you to pause as well. When we're speaking Serbian, they're supposed to interpret. Does this statement reflect exactly what you said?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: Exactly everything I said was written in that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you here today, would your answers to these questions essentially be the same?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: I hope they would be the same. Perhaps I could not repeat everything in the same order, but at any rate it would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, may I tender this package, the statement and eight documents that have not been admitted and then there's some that have been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, with respect to two documents referred to in para 13, i.e., 1D800 and the other referred to by the ERN number, I don't think they are either updated or translated into English. So in order for you to tender to those -- those two documents, you need to put that -- those documents to the witness live. Otherwise, do you have any objection, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Otherwise, no, Mr. President. I would note that what is currently listed as 1D00841 and for which presumably a Defence exhibit number is sought is already admitted as P00737.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Should we give the number to the witness's Rule 92 ter statement first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D6801 becomes Exhibit D2530, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And as regards the six other documents, associated exhibits, the numbers will be given in due course by the Registrar. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I would like to read out the summary of Mr. Zdravko Cvoro's statement. I'll read it out in the English language. [In English] Zdravko Cvoro was the president of the Crisis Staff of the Pale municipality. From the 1st of January, 1992, to the 31st of August, 1992, he was the president of the Executive Committee of the Pale municipality. He was never a member of the SDS. At the start of the war, the majority of the population living in Pale was Serbs and a large number of Serb refugees moved from Sarajevo to Pale. The municipality had difficulties in providing the refugees with accommodation and humanitarian aid and all measures were taken to provide them with the accommodation and basic living conditions. During the war a number of incidents caused fear of retaliation and insecurity among the Muslim population in Pale, as crimes were committed by their compatriots. These included the killing and wounding of Pale SJB policemen, then the massacre of JNA soldiers and VRS soldiers who were transporting food and other supplies, and the killing and expulsion of a large number of Serbs. As a result, there were individual and subsequently collective requests to move out from Pale to Sarajevo. Zdravko Cvoro, along with the president of the Pale municipality, personally went to neighbourhoods inhabited by Muslims to convince them to stay and assured them that as municipal officials they would guarantee their safety. The Pale municipality confirmed it would ensure that Muslims would enjoy all civil rights and normal living conditions. Despite this, a large number of requests to move were received and at a meeting of 18th of June, 1992, a decision was made by the Pale municipality Assembly acknowledging the constitutional right to freedom of movement and residence. There was no forced expulsion of civilians of Muslim and Croatian ethnicity from Pale. Those that left did so at their own request and out of their own free will. Many left in organised convoys and took personal belongings. Others made agreements with Serb neighbours in relation to the safekeeping of their property. Those residents who did not wish to leave continued to live together with the Serbs. There was no destruction of non-Serb property in this area, except along the demarcation line and where there was combat activity. The Pale municipality Executive Committee drew up a document requiring the SJB, police station, to undertake the protection of property of non-Serbs until it is taken over by the authorised municipal commission, as well as one regarding the establishment of a commission for refugees and humanitarian aid. After the war immovable property was returned to owners and a number of Muslims returned to their homes. Pale Crisis Staff was put in place in case of the regular authorities were unable to meet. The Crisis Staff was composed of more or less the same people who were in the regular bodies. The difference was in the way of work, in the sense that regular authorities used to have a period of up to 15 days to make decisions, while the Crisis Staff had to respond in urgent situations, for instance, in an hour's time. According to the instructions of the Presidency of the SFRY, Yugoslavia, the republics had an obligation to develop plans for emergency and the managers of those plans were the Crisis Staffs. In the event of a natural disaster or other emergency situations, the Crisis Staff was convened with the most responsible members of the municipality as its members. According to the law on Territorial Defence at that time, private resources necessary for the functioning of the authority could be employed. The situation was dramatic in terms of telephone lines in Pale. There was a grave deficiency in the -- this aspect. Resultantly, both Serbs and Muslims had their telephones switched off for this reason. In addition, the army switched off telephones of other state authorities, including the Ministry of Justice. During the war, the Muslim municipality of Pale was formed, which included Renovica and Praca and other Muslim villages. If the VRS wanted to take over the Muslim municipality of Pale, it could easily have done so, but it did not because the Muslim population was a majority there. The Muslim community of Pale still exists today with its base in Praca. In Pale, in the centre, there was a Catholic church which had been preserved to this day, while there has never been a mosque in Pale itself. [Interpretation] That would be the summary in view of your decision. Could we please call up in e-court 1D800, the one that I'm supposed to deal with live with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cvoro, could you please take a look at this and tell us what this report refers to, this SRNA report at the time. Would you like me to read it out or would you like to read it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: As far as I can see, this has to do with the destruction of certain lines that were linked with Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is the date of this report?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: The 28th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what does it say in the second paragraph? Can you read all of it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: "Four sniper shots destroyed the mini link on the building of the telegraph and the telephone in the street Vojvoda Putnika 100. From the moment when telephone traffic was disrupted until the present day, digital links work at only 30 per cent of their capacity."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us where this street is, Vojvoda Putnika, and what this building is?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: It is in Sarajevo. It is the main street that runs by the Marsal Tito barracks, the former Marsal Tito barracks, and it goes towards the Malta neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So how did this reflect on the state of the telephone lines in Pale?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: Well, we had enough trouble as it was in terms of the number of telephone lines. Pale was a small municipality that had small telephone capacities. As these links were destroyed, the situation became much worse and it was very hard to begin with, the situation regarding telephone lines, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how did you resolve that, in view of the fact that the state organs had their seat there and then there was television and so on, how did you resolve that problem?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: When the state organs, or rather, the republic organs moved to Pale, major problems were created. First of all, they were supposed to be provided with accommodation and telephone lines and other lines. In addition to the republican organs, the SRNA news agency appeared asking for proper premises and telephone lines so that they could function. We were covered by Sarajevo. All the information that we received we received as they wished. The then-appointed director Todor Dutina came to see me and asked me to do whatever I could in order to establish the SRNA news agency. I asked him, "Well, what have you got Todor?" And he said, "I've got nothing." "What do you need, Todor?" And his answer was, "I need an office, a telephone, and a typewriter." I was president of the Executive Board and from my very own office I gave Mr. Dutina a telephone with a Telefax and also a telephone number and a typewriter. Then he went on to establish the SRNA news agency. Many Serbs came to Pale. Among others, there were people who were familiar with this line of work. They quickly made do and established the SRNA news agency. The situation was similar as far as television was concerned too. Many people asked for telephone lines or telephone numbers. Also in Pale we also had only primary medical care. All of that was based in the health centre there and the wounded and ill already started coming in. A reserve war time hospital arrived in Pale and we gave them premises within the Koran hotel and that is where we established a military war time hospital. Also, many telephone numbers were required by this hospital. I also know full well that for the government and the Presidency and the Assembly, we practically mobilised all the telephone numbers that were not indispensable, both in the business sector and the social services. It's not only that there weren't enough telephone lines. There weren't enough telephone sets as such. From the municipality and from Famos, we got all the telephone sets and started using them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document receives number D2531, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D25730, can we see that briefly. It's marked with an ERN number in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since there's no translation, Mr. Cvoro, I shall deal with this very quickly, these communications, that is. So in the fourth line from above Slobodan Aviljas is calling the Crisis Staff and introduces himself by saying that as the Minister of Justice, Slobo Aviljas. Did you know him and did he work at the Ministry of Justice?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him personally, and we actually did our military service together before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Further down it says Slobodan Aviljas, Aco Kutlaca is the interlocutor. It says: "Listen, I am in the post office right now. I'm calling here from the hospital. Somebody disconnected the telephone of the duty judges up there where we are sleeping." Further down Kutlaca says: "Let me tell you, this was disconnected on orders from the commander. You have to submit a request in writing in order to be reconnected." How come this happened? Is this in line with what you told us about, that you had these problems and that you even disconnected the telephone of the Ministry of Justice?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: This confirms what I said, that we disconnected the telephones of many institutions. Among others, this thing happened too and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt the witness, but I think this is in line with the guidance the accused received before about questions that are necessarily leading. This has been throughout a kind of an invitation for witnesses to -- presenting material to him that we can't even read in full and then leading the witness to what the point that Dr. Karadzic wants him to affirm. Under the circumstances, I certainly didn't object to the attempt to use the document, but I think it needs to be used fairly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you follow, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I would like to respond. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can rephrase, but the fact remains that the Prosecution is reading only parts of documents to witnesses and then I have to spend my time in re-direct. And of course I can rephrase this. I can just ask: How does this read in terms of your own experience?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Am I supposed to say something? You're asking me, President, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, if the Trial Chamber allows me to do so, I'm asking you how this reads in terms of your own experience with insufficient number of telephone lines?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, given the -- this Trial Chamber's practice as regards the admission of intercepts, I don't think there's a point on your part to putting this witness -- to the witness. Why don't you just elicit from the witness directly as to the telephone situation without having to rely on this intercept. We have difficulty following this line of questioning without the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. Maybe I can ask this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, before you -- if you start your question: Is it correct, that is a leading question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. Thank you. Everything you said is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, who was it that you denied telephone lines for the needs of the state organs and on what basis did you do that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: Well, look, the federal law on defence regulated things as follows. In case of war or imminent threat of war, all resources can be mobilised, all resources that can be used for the defence of the country, or rather, the defence of the territory involved. That means that in addition to the resources that the army has, that the business community has, even personal resources can be mobilised for the defence of the state or the defence of the territory, in keeping with that, even in peace time conditions according to that law, when military exercises are carried out, it wasn't only military conscripts that were mobilised. Also materiel resources were mobilised, such as vehicles, scooters, motorboats, and other resources that are needed for military exercises. In war time the situation is even more drastic. So the situation that we had to deal with was that we could not function, that we could not meet all these needs that had cropped up, so we disconnected telephones of Serbs too. I as president of the Executive Board did not have a telephone either; that is to say, I gave up my own telephone so that other organs could function, Serbs, companies, some of the Muslims who had received this order. I can say that I did not even sign this order, but I'm trying to explain what the reasons were for this order. It is provided here as a document bearing my name and surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If you don't wish to it admit this intercept which just proves that the ministry was also left without a telephone, then I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Cvoro, as you have noted, your evidence in chief was admitted mainly in written form in view of your oral testimony. Now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. I want to speak to you first about this aspect of your statement and it concerns these paragraphs. I want to talk to you about the portions of your statement which assert that Muslims became insecure because they feared retaliation for what their "compatriots" had done, that's paragraph 4. And so they sought to leave, although Serb officials tried to convince them to stay, that's paragraphs 5 through 6. So they left of their own free will, paragraph 6, in organised convoys with their personal belongings and documents, and they protected their property by entering into various agreements with their Serb neighbours or through other arrangements, that's paragraphs 7 through 8. And I want to look at your assertion that Muslims left voluntarily of their own free will. This Court has heard evidence, Mr. Cvoro, that, among other things, the Bosnian Serb police in Pale harassed, threatened, or pressured Muslims to leave, and that's found at P0733, paragraphs 23 through 27, 33 through 34, 39, and 49. Mr. Cvoro, that was, in fact, part of the reality that Muslims faced that made their departure not an act of free will and not voluntary; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, the police was not under the jurisdiction of the local authorities. I didn't have any authority over the police. They have their vertical chain of structure. That was the case before the war and that is the case nowadays. My only influence on the police would be in the form of a request or a recommendation. There was no other way for me to influence the work of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well -- and I'll talk with you a bit further about that in a bit, Mr. Cvoro. But for the moment I simply want to confirm, as I think you impliedly did, that, in fact, the police in Pale, that is, the Bosnian Serb police, engaged in efforts to force Muslims out?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: I am not aware of that; however, we provided document D28 which shows that the municipality of Pale in response to the written request of the Muslims to move out responded to it and that happened somewhere in early April. They said that there was no reason for them to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, I know there are other documents and I see you want to direct our attention to another issue. I'm focusing on the actions of the police. Now, you said you weren't aware of that, but the fact is, Mr. Cvoro, that that's exactly what you said in 1992, that the police were engaged in such conduct. And I want to turn your attention to D00031, a meeting of the Pale Municipal Assembly on the 18th of June, 1992. But, in fact, before we go there I want to point out -- I want to show you and I want you to tell the Court how that meeting came about, so let's turn to D0030, a document of 12 June 1992.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: What document is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It will be shown on the screen to you, sir. It should be in front of you right now.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: This is Mr. Starcevic, the president of the municipality. He is sending it to the secretary of the Pale SDS. I was a representative of the executive branch and the president of the municipality --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, and I don't mean to raise my voice but I'm trying to move us along quickly, so I only did that -- it's the only way I know how to stop you for a moment. I want you to confirm that this document is, in fact, a message from the president of the Pale Municipal Assembly, Starcevic, who is asking the secretary of the Pale SDS to urgently call a meeting of the Pale SDS Main Board so that the party can adopt a general position on the moving out of non-Serbian population from Pale. And he notes that if the Main Board, that is, the SDS Main Board, can meet as soon as possible then a session of the Municipal Assembly can be called for 18 June 1992. Now, as far as you're aware, that's what happened on June 12th, that Mr. Starcevic pushed the --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And in fact in terms of the link or the interconnection between the municipality and the party, I'd also like to turn to 65 ter 24210. And we'll get to the 18 June meeting in just a moment. This is a document dated 26th of May, 1992. It bears your signature. It's a request for allotment of funds --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: Yes, addressed to the government of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we continue on to page -- the next page of the English, please, it includes some of the expenditures of the municipality. And we see -- we have to continue to the next page of the English, I'm sorry, or just scroll down, please, on the English so the Judges can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps if we turn to page -- the next page in the English as well, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We see at the top of the -- toward the top of the page in English a payment to the Serb Democratic Party Pale of 100.000 dinars, I take it. And if we turn to the next page in English, we see in the middle of the page funding of the Serb Democratic Party Pale has been stated according to their needs. So this document, sir, is a reflection of the financial support by the municipality to the Pale SDS?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, in the regular budget there were always allocations intended for the financing of political parties. Therefore, there is nothing illegal in this because the SDS party was a party that had absolute power in Pale. The individuals who held official positions, most of them were appointed by the party. This is only a request for the provision of fund to finance only one portion, and that is specifically the costs in the month of May. One can see the breakdown of the funds and what the needs are, and that's the difference. Obviously there was a need to provide a small portion of financing to the party as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's adequate, Mr. Cvoro.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I tender that document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 24210 becomes Exhibit P6029, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could now turn to the June 18th meeting which is D00031. Now, there appear to be two items on the agenda, Mr. Cvoro, as reflected on page 2 of the English. The first item is a report on the security situation and, as we see in the document, Lieutenant-Colonel Krstic takes the floor at one point and reports. But the second item is the one referred to in the document we saw earlier from Mr. Starcevic, and that is position to be taken by the Assembly on non-Serbs moving out of the territory of Pale municipality. And if we turn to item 2 which is located on the -- begins on the fourth page of the English and I believe the same page in B/C/S. We can see that there are various opinions provided by the attendees ranging from the view that the government should first pass a decision and the municipality would follow that to that there should be exchanges that govern the transfer to UNPROFOR should handle it and so on. But I wanted to look at what was stated at the bottom of the page in English by the president of the municipality and the chairman of the Executive Committee. Now, the chairman of the Executive Committee is you, Mr. Cvoro; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And there you and the president of the Assembly object to the activities of the public security station, that's the police, because it had participated in the attempt to organise the Muslims and move them out. You go on to say that was before a political decision had been made and thus bypassing the official structures of power. Now, Mr. Cvoro, that's a reflection in 1992 of the fact -- of your awareness of the activities of the police to get Muslims out of Pale; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: No, we were not satisfied with some of the work on the ground done by the police, and we sent a request, or rather, a protest demanding that this situation be rectified. I cannot say generally that the police was involved in such activities because I have no knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the issue of the moving out of the Muslims which is item 2 of this agenda and which was raised by Mr. Starcevic, that was not a concern or issue that was isolated to Pale. In fact, the issue of the moving out of the Muslims was being addressed elsewhere in RS by RS officials; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I know about Pale and I can guarantee you that there was no forced moving out of the Muslims from Pale. We did our best by going on the ground. I myself went two or three times to the villages where Muslims lived and I tried to persuade them --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Cvoro, sorry, that's in your statement and I'm trying to use our time as efficiently as we can. My question was about whether or not the issue of moving out of the Muslims was simply something that arose in Pale or was being addressed in other parts of the RS. And in that connection I'd like to turn to 65 ter 00580.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we're doing that I think that the witness should in general be allowed to complete his answers because it's -- if there's a shortage of time, it's not really an excuse to be rude to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. It just occurred to me how the terms would be translated into B/C/S. When we say "moving out," it may be transitive verb and intransitive verb. Is there a difference?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I do take the point -- the Court's point, and so I'm trying to rely on the translations provided, and then I think we can, among other things, rely on the totality of the evidence to understand the meaning of the term. But in terms of the strict usage of that term in English, I'm attempting to follow the translations I've been provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, bearing that in mind, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, with respect to Mr. Robinson's issue, time is a concern for a variety of reasons which I'm happy to identify for the Court, but my -- my moments of interrupting the witness are a reflection of that. So if -- given the nature of this week and the fact that we will have down time this week because of the number of witnesses that will be -- that translated, I'm more than willing to be less vigilant about curtailing the witness if I'm assured that I'm not going to be unfairly held to a -- an arbitrary limit, provided that I'm focusing on relevant materials, as I'm clearly doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we leave the matter there and could you -- could you ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Because it was my impression that the witness was not following your question properly, probably because of the translation issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's give it a try again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, just to make sure we're talking about the same matter, we had looked a few moments ago at Mr. Starcevic's request for a position by the Pale SDS Main Board about the moving out of the Muslims. We had looked at the agenda item on the 18 June Municipal Assembly session. An item which provided -- which asked -- for which the agenda was position to be taken by the Assembly on non-Serbs moving out of the territory. And then my question for you was about whether this -- in fact, I was stating to you the fact that this issue concerning the moving out of the Muslims was not one that arose in Pale only but that was being addressed elsewhere in the RS. And you said that you were not -- you claimed that you were not aware of that as I understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just, that's the problem with paraphrasing. If Mr. Robinson thinks that's a problem, then he can read out where we are now. I'm trying to bring the witness up-to-date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's make the question simpler. So what is your question, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll repeat what I said verbatim before Mr. Robinson made his objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: My question was whether the issue of the moving out of the Muslims was simply something that arose in Pale or was being addressed in other parts of the RS. And that had been --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, as far as other parts of the RS are concerned, I don't know. I was the representative of the executive branch. The initiative for the moving out was launched by the Muslims themselves. They came to see me both individually and in groups. They also came to see Mr. Starcevic. Mr. Starcevic then --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I am going to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: -- launched an initiative to address this issue --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Witness.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: -- at the highest level at the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think you answered the question, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- Cvoro. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The witness answered the question and then proceeded to repeat various parts of his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Witness, I want you to look at this exhibit. This is an article from Javnost and it refers to the government of the Serbian autonomous region of Birac, and specifically in the second paragraph it refers to a decision passed on the "safe moving of Muslims from that area." The suggestion to the neighbouring Muslim-Croat municipalities to organise this within seven days. And the reason given by the government to take that step, as it says, as a result of crimes Muslim extremists carried out against Serbs in this area. Now, Mr. Cvoro, this is, is it not, a reflection -- and this is, by the way, the 6th of June, as you can see, this is a reflection of the same discussion that you alluded to going on in other parts of the RS at approximately the same time; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: This has nothing to do with this text. This is the first time that I see it and I can categorically assert that I'm not familiar with this manner. This was beyond my scope of responsibility. I was addressing the problems relating to the Muslims in Pale and that was all. That was my task and my objective and I think that I successfully achieved it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Very well. I'll move on --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But I tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. This is a classic example of something that cannot be admitted because it doesn't directly contradict the witness. It isn't written by or for anybody within his purview or his sphere. So he wouldn't be expected to know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: However, did the witness not say that he didn't know whether similar things were happening in other regions?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, and this doesn't contradict that whatsoever. If similar things were happening in other regions, that's one thing. But if he knew -- the question is whether he knew, and this doesn't shed light on that at all. If it was something he would be expected to have seen, such as something in his municipality, in his organ, okay, it should be admitted. But simply the way this is so general and so unconnected to his own duties and position that it's not admissible in our view.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger, would you like to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, I do wish to respond. That is an inaccurate and unduly restrictive interpretation of impeachment. This witness -- I mean, it certainly is possible to impeach a witness -- and by the way, I would like to ask if the witness -- I think we've been a little bit too lax about arguing objections in front of witnesses, so we may want to determine whether this witness speaks English; and if he does not, then I think we should continue the discussion with his headphones off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, it's certainly possible to impeach a witness with direct evidence, that the activities he says he engaged in are contradicted by the documents, but the reality here is that this witness is not being proffered for a travel log of his own -- merely his own activities during the war. He's being proffered to show that this was -- that what happened in Pale was spontaneous, voluntary, and unrelated to any policy by the leadership. And his -- apart from the fact that given his proximity, his physical proximity, to the leadership in Pale gives rise to at least a realistic impeachment of the claim that he didn't know anything about what was happening elsewhere. It also is a contradiction of the general proposition raised by the Defence in proffering this witness at all; that is, this is a purely isolated individual municipality thing that had nothing to do with policy. And we surely are entitled to combat that with evidence that it was happening across the RS. And I would note also, and I'll be happy to take it up with the witness, that 65 ter 15087 reveals clearly that Javnost is a party organ and so there is that additional confirmation. This is information that the party wanted to disseminate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I, Excellency? I'll respond in English. This witness hasn't been invited for the purpose that Mr. Tieger said, but for the purpose of refuting what was done by the Prosecution concerning this very municipality, which is in the indictment. And this is the top of the executive power in this municipality, very responsible man and very responsible authority, who was not a member of SDS. And I don't see any reason to go throughout Republika Srpska. We are dealing with this municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber finds the document to be relevant to the credibility of the witness and will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 00580 receives number P6030, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cvoro, for your co-operation. Please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, continuing in connection with the issues raised by the paragraphs in your statement that I alluded to at the outset, this Trial Chamber has also heard evidence that another factor leading Muslims in Pale to conclude that they had no choice but to leave was the arrival in Pale of badly beaten Muslim civilians who had been expelled from Bratunac in May 1992 and which was one way that Muslims in Pale learned what was in store if they didn't leave "voluntarily." Now, I'd like you to look at a few moments of P3206, a video.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Cvoro, do you recognise these battered men as among the group of Muslims that were -- that passed through Pale in the middle of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I don't know anything about who brought these Muslims to Pale by what means and who sent them on. I do know that we reacted promptly. We gathered the Crisis Staff and went to see someone from the authorities, trying to tell them that such things ought not happen in Pale and that these Muslims have to be released, or rather, allowed to join their compatriots. Thanks to the president and the prime minister, this was done quickly. As far as I am concerned, I was not involved in any of it. I didn't know about it. I was just awakened in the middle of the night by the police who said, "We have many Muslims who were brought in Pale by someone and left there." Do you know what it means to bring someone and leave them there in that situation? Could we have done anything other than accommodate them and provide them with the basic necessities as well as to ask that they go to where they belonged? This was indeed done promptly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just for the record, Mr. President, that went from 00.53 to 001:39.5. The Crisis Staff was directed by the government to transport those prisoners out of Pale and into Muslim territory; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: I don't know who was in charge of that activity, but I do know that security was provided by the police and other units. They left Pale safely. There was also a problem how to secure means of transport and how to accommodate them. How to move them securely. We found certain trucks where they could be put on so that they wouldn't cause problems or that some Serbs wouldn't do anything stupid. As far as I know, they arrived there and they reported themselves there and were safe and sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber, Mr. Cvoro, has also heard evidence that yet another reason why the Muslims who departed Pale did not feel they had any real choice but to leave was the presence of notorious paramilitaries not only in the municipality but actually "put up at the Panorama Hotel," and that's P0733 paragraphs 39 through 40. And that too, Mr. Cvoro, was part of the reality of Pale, correct, that notorious paramilitary figures were put up at the Panorama Hotel?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: I had no contact with such forces. At the Panorama there were refugees from Croatia. They were accommodated at the Panorama. In 1994 we also received a great number of refugees from Croatia who stayed there until late May.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Later on we were unable to accommodate them any further and we sent them on to Serbia. I don't know of any paramilitary organisations or armed forces who were there at the time. I did not meet such people, and I'm very sorry but I can't help you on this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's look quickly at P01107, a document dated the 10th of August, 1992. And if we turn to the next page in English, please. Next page, please, I'm sorry. As you see at the top: "It was stated that while inspecting the Pale public security station that a group of 'Arkanovci' are still present at the 'Panorama' Hotel. Chief Koroman presents that as a solved problem because he is expecting their commander in a couple of days with whom he would solve it without a problem." And I think you've seen the cover page of this document, Mr. Cvoro. This is a reflection, is it not, of the presence of paramilitary figures put up at the Panorama Hotel in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: I tell you again, in August there was the Executive Council. I was the main person in the executive authority. I had no jurisdiction over the police. The army and the police had their own affairs and I did not meddle in that. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, the Trial Chamber's also heard evidence, again I'm referring to those portions of your statement indicating that Muslims left of their own free will, evidence that one of the reasons why the Muslims in Pale felt they did not have a free choice about whether to leave was because Nikola Koljevic, one of the members of the collective Presidency at that time and who later assumed the position of vice-president of RS, essentially encouraged them to leave by telling them they were not wanted and, therefore, should not stay, that's P0733, paragraph 38. Now, I note that was -- that's not something included in your statement. Do you purport to be aware of Mr. Koljevic's positions regarding population transfers?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I am not familiar with that and I don't know how I could control Mr. Koljevic in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, then I'll move on. For the benefit of the Chamber I would refer, among other things, to P00986 and P00794.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay, that is a bit of an argument, I understand. But that has been done in the past for -- in order to avoid confronting the witness, but I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Cvoro, in paragraph 15 of your statement, you say that some people came to verify the agreements concerning property, regarding protecting each other's property. And you emphasise in your -- in paragraph 15 that this applied to both Serbs and non-Serbs, and I understand this to be your effort to show that people were independently interested in leaving and so some of them came to the municipality just to make sure that their agreements would be honoured. Is that basically it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: You see, this is how it was. Pale is a small community. Muslims and Serbs knew each other well. Many Serbs and many Muslims who lived in Sarajevo had their own homes, houses, and apartments. When the Serbs arrived in Pale, they had acquaintances and lifelong friends with whom they stayed in contact. People tried to protect their property. The Serbs who had already left and the Muslims who were supposed to leave got together. They came to the municipality to legalise such arrangements. We did not accept that because there was no legal basis under the war time circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Cvoro, the fact of the matter is that non-Serbs who sought to leave were not permitted to do so until a list of their property was made and that property taken over by the municipality; isn't that the reality why people came to the municipality --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at P00738, please.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: P738 is a document dated the 6th of July, 1992. And it bears your signature as well as the signature of the commander of the civilian protection staff, Mr. Blagojevic. And it provides that the Pale police station is requested to take immediate measures to protect the property of non-Serbian inhabitants who have moved out of the territory until this property is taken over by an authorised municipal commission. And it provides in part 2: "Individuals or families of non-Serbian ethnicities who wish to leave the territory of Pale municipality must not be allowed to do so until a list of their property is made and the property is taken over in accordance with the regulations in force ..." So contrary to the suggestion in paragraph 15 of your statement, Mr. Cvoro, this document is directed at the non-Serbian population and compels them to deal with municipal officials to make sure that a list of their property is made and provided to those officials; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: You see, we informed the police station to secure such parts of territory where there were non-Serb residents, given the fact that there had already come in some requests for their moving out. We organised municipal commissions which were to take over responsibility for the property left behind by the Muslims. The station was only included from the point of view of security of people working in the field. The commissions in question had to make up lists of property and inventory left behind by the Muslims. Also in item 2 it became a problem that many Muslims - I cannot speak for the Croats because they did not move out, they remained in Pale - but many left without a hand-over and there was a problem. The problem was that there were people trying to steal that property. That is why we informed the police station to secure the property. The civilian protection staff commander was in charge of gathering -- actually, of securing the property and preserving both movable and immovable assets.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when you talk about securing and preserving the property, and when you refer in your statement to protecting that property at paragraph 6 or 7 or 15, that protection was not for the Muslims who had given up the property so they could leave the municipality, but it was protection so that the property would end up in the hands of the commodity reserves of Republika Srpska? That's where that property was going? Yes or no and then I want to direct you to a couple of documents in connection with that.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: Property was protected, although I can't say it was 100 per cent. There was looting. We tried our best to protect all property, movable and immovable. The greatest problem was immovable property. We tried to have it gathered in one place and stored, be it in the garrison command premises or in some other institutions. In charge of all that was the civilian protection staff. We weren't too pleased with the work of those commissions, and later on we established audit commissions because there were abuses. And the audit commissions were in charge of screening what the real situation was in the field and where those abuses occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Cvoro, we still have the document of the 6th of July up there, and why don't we look at the preamble which provides that: "Pursuant to Article 86 of the Statute of Pale municipality," which I presume invests -- or vests the chairman of the Executive Board and others with appropriate authority, "and the instructions of the Government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina regulating the distribution of war booty ..." So this document and the conclusions reflected in it, including the fact that non-Serbs who wished to leave will not be permitted to do so until a list of their property is made, is pursuant to the government regulations on collecting war booty. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: I wouldn't call it war booty. In any case, we wanted to protect that property so that it didn't go to people who didn't need it. Only by having a proper list could we gain a clear insight into what the situation was like in the field. That's why we established such commissions which were tasked with creating appropriate lists.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not who didn't need it, it says -- it should be who it did not belong in terms of rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's be clear on what this document refers to. It refers to the instructions of the government of regulating the distribution of war booty. So let's look quickly at two documents. One of those is already in evidence, P05502.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies, I was only trying to say that the words in line 21 are not interpreted accurately. The witness said that the property was kept safe so that it wouldn't go to those who had no right to enjoy it. And not to those "who didn't need it."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: These are the July 13th instructions and the implementation of the decree concerning war booty. And in particular I direct your attention to the first line of the -- item 1, which refers to the fact that this regulates in greater detail the application and means of implementation of the earlier decree, which was number 8 of the Official Gazette/892, number 8 of the Official Gazette 1992, and in that connection I would turn your attention to 65 ter 17747, which is number 8 of the Official Gazette of 1992. And we can see from the last page and you can see it there on the Serbian that that's dated the 2nd of June, 1992, and it provides, among other things, in Article 2 that a municipal commission will be set up to receive the valuables, that commission will keep them until they are delivered to the treasury of the national bank of the Serbian Republic of BiH, or Article 5 which provides that the municipal commission shall take care of the movable property and assets pending their delivery to the republic's emergency reserves. So this is the document concerning war booty and regulating the distribution of war booty to which the preamble of P738, that is, the July 6 document refers; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: It is a governmental decree which was binding on all organs of the authorities for all organs of the executive branch. I see nothing that is in dispute there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender that document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit 6031.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Cvoro, the commission referred to in Exhibit 6031 that we just looked at, that is, the commission that is supposed to take care of the movable property and assets pending delivery to the republic's emergency reserves is reflected in D00034. And I'd like you to look at that quickly. This is a document dated the 14th of July which bears your signature, Cvoro, and it refers to the fact that given -- the conclusion that given the fact that the central commission and subcommissions in charge of making a list of movable and immovable property of non-Serbian citizens have not completed their tasks and there have been resulting problems. So that document, Mr. Cvoro, refers to the commission which is envisioned by the government decree we looked at a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: This first and foremost has to do with the commission established by the Executive Board, that is, the previous commission. We were not happy with the work of that commission and it is stated here that given the fact that the central commission and subcommissions in charge of making a list of movable and immovable property of non-Serb citizens who have left Pale municipality have not fully completed their tasks. And as I have explained a moment ago, we established a separate audit commission to check the work of the previous commission and what had been done, so as to come up with the appropriate results, the real results. The problem were rural areas where Muslims had lived, where there was plenty of abandoned cattle, and that was where the focus was. There was a lot of misappropriation and we were not happy with that segment of their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we adjourn for today?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You will continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You will have about ten minutes tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, ten minutes won't quite do. I've been really -- I can tell you that I marked this out very, very carefully, and I can advise the Court of several factors which make it much different, if the Court needs that information, but I don't think I'll need a great deal of time but I certainly more than ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Tomorrow morning at 9.00. Mr. Cvoro, we'll adjourn for today and continue tomorrow, but in the meantime you are not supposed to discuss with anybody else about your testimony. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 5th day of December, 2012, at 9.00 a.m.
